reviewNotes: Source title is “…”. Descriptive study title Two Pawns Against a Rook begins after ...Ke8 at 141 seconds (five pieces). Three checked branches compare Kg8 shouldering, losing g7 ...Kf7, and drawing Kh8. Corrected the source’s draw claim after g7 ...Kf7: it loses because Kf7 protects g8. Promotion/capture completion is explicitly independent. Earlier rook sacrifice remains context.
transcript: Rook takes eight check, a brilliant sacrifice that has to be accepted because the rook and [music] the king are lined up. But after the king takes, all that white is left with are two pawns against one rook. And this black rook is already attacking one of the two pawns. So white, of course, pushes it and tries to get it close enough to get a new queen. But black is not naive enough to allow that. But nonetheless, black has to be careful. If we start, for example, with a check, now after the king goes to the corner, there is literally no way for black to prevent G7 and G8 queen. So black has to be a little bit more sophisticated than just throwing a bunch of checks. What else can black do? If the rook goes behind the pawn, now after F6, black is preparing to bring the king like this. And if you keep pushing the pawn, now actually this is a draw. The king and the rook collaborate in stopping the promotion. And moving the king doesn't achieve anything. Black can just wait because whenever you push this pawn, he's just going to collect like this and then sacrifice the rook for the last pawn. And this is going to be a draw. But white [music] is not that naive. And instead of just pushing this pawn, he would spend a move to play king to F7 to shoulder the black king so that now the G pawn can promote [music] and white would win. So rook to F4 doesn't work. So is white just going to win with these two pawns? Well, it's not that easy. Black does have a very ingenious plan. King to D8. And now after white starts pushing, there is rook to C8. And this very odd setup prepares to meet F7 with king to E7. >> [music] >> And now we achieve that same setup where the rook and the king are preventing [music] the promotion. But white foresees all of this. And instead of just pushing the pawn, plays the incredibly precise and brilliant king to H7, threatening to promote the G pawn, but again, black can prevent that [music] idea with king to E8. And now if you push the pawn, black is going to sit in front of the F pawn and prevent the promotion of the G pawn. So this would be a draw. And going to the corner would allow king to D7 with a discovered check and a transposition to the drawing line. So is this it? Is black finally out of the woods? Well, not exactly. White plays the cold-blooded king to G8, gaining a position with the black king and allowing the king to move away with a discovered check. This allows white to now play king to F7 and shoulder the black king, meaning that it is now going to be pretty much impossible to stop the G pawn. And one last precise move that doesn't allow this rook sacrifice is going to be king to G6, which means that white will [music] finally be able to get a win and win this game.
